Seif katan 2, "one may not place," etc., because it is possible to shake it off. See siman 277, seif 3, where it is explained that if one forgot a wax candle on a table, he may shake the table and the candle will fall. It is written there that even if the candle is lit, he may shake the table, provided that he does not intend to extinguish it.

This is not comparable to oil, which cannot be shaken away without loss, because the oil would have to be shaken onto the ground and would be ruined. If he shook it into another vessel, he would instead render that second vessel unusable on Shabbos.

"According to the view in siman 309, seif 4," etc. That view holds that the permission to shake off muktzeh applies specifically where the forbidden item was forgotten on the permitted object, not where it was deliberately placed there before Shabbos. Where it was deliberately placed, the permitted object itself becomes a basis for the prohibited item and may not be moved. Nevertheless, when he placed it there with the intention that it not remain there for the entire Shabbos, it can be treated like a forgotten item and may be shaken off.

"And so writes Ran," etc. The wording is not precise if it implies that Ran forbids for the same reason as the first opinion in siman 309. Their reasons differ. According to that first opinion, the prohibition is that the vessel became a basis for a prohibited item. According to Ran, the prohibition is that one may not render a vessel unusable even for part of Shabbos. Beit Yosef's words, "and so writes Ran," refer only to the practical ruling that Ran too prohibits.

"It requires study, for everyone agrees that if he placed it there on Shabbos it is permitted," this is the correct text. Beit Yosef sought to prohibit for 2 reasons: first, according to the first opinion in siman 309, because deliberate placement creates a basis; second, according to Ran, because it is forbidden to render a vessel unusable even for part of Shabbos. Magen Avraham rejects the first reason: where the prohibited item was not upon the vessel at bein hashmashot, even that opinion does not treat the vessel as a basis.

"This is an explicit Gemara," meaning Shabbos 154b. Rav Huna says that where one's animal was carrying glass vessels, the Gemara establishes the case as small bloodletters' horns, which are repulsive and muktzeh. They may not be removed directly by hand. Leaving them on the animal causes pain to the animal, while loosening the sacks and allowing them to fall would break them and cause monetary loss. Therefore one brings cushions and pillows, places them underneath, loosens the ropes, and allows the sacks to fall onto the cushions so that they do not break. The Gemara asks that this renders the cushions unusable, and answers that the case involves small bundles that can be shaken off the cushions. Large bundles are forbidden because their weight prevents shaking them off.

If deliberate placement during Shabbos itself made the cushions a basis for the entire Shabbos, even the small bundles should be forbidden, because after placing them on the cushions he could not shake them off. The Gemara's permission therefore proves that an item placed there during Shabbos does not create the status of a basis in this manner.

"Rather Ran," etc., still holds that it is forbidden to render a vessel unusable even for part of Shabbos, except in a case of substantial loss. Thus Magen Avraham rejects Beit Yosef's first reason but leaves the second reason in place.

The discussion concerning sparks is different. Sparks extinguish immediately after falling into the vessel, so the vessel is unavailable only for an extremely brief moment and immediately becomes usable again. The Gemara therefore permits placing a vessel beneath sparks. By contrast, where a candle or another muktzeh item rests on the vessel for a meaningful period, the vessel is unavailable for that interval.

One must also distinguish between a case in which the prohibited item can be shaken off at once and a case in which it cannot. Where it can be shaken off, the vessel does not remain unusable and there is greater room for leniency. Where the item cannot be removed until later, the prohibition of rendering the vessel unusable applies.

The principle is therefore that an object does not become a basis merely because muktzeh was newly placed upon it during Shabbos, but one may still violate the separate prohibition of making a permitted vessel unavailable for use. In a case of substantial monetary loss, the authorities permit more, as explained in the sources cited by Magen Avraham.

(12) "One may place a vessel." Even on Shabbos. (13) "To catch the sparks." Meaning the flame or sparks dripping from the lamp, so that whatever is beneath it will not catch fire. (14) "Actual sparks." This means sparks that go out immediately. It is therefore permitted to move the vessel even after the sparks have fallen into it, and there is no issue of rendering the vessel unusable even for a short time. The ash of the sparks themselves, however, may not be moved because it is nolad. [Magen Avraham; see Eliyah Rabbah] (15) "Even before Shabbos." Although regarding other melachot we rule that it is permitted to begin the process before Shabbos even though the melacha is completed on Shabbos, as stated at the beginning of siman 252, and we do not decree lest one begin it on Shabbos, here the matter is different because extinguishing is directly caused by the arrangement. [Hagahot at the end of chapter Kirah and other authorities] (16) "Because he brings," etc. Where there is danger of fire, it is permitted to place a vessel full of water to receive the sparks. Likewise, if he sees that a lamp is about to fall upon a table, in a pressing situation there is room to place water in a manner that prevents danger, subject to the distinctions stated by the authorities. (17) "And he should not do so on Shabbos," etc. Pouring water into the receptacle in which a wax or tallow candle stands, so that when the flame reaches the level of the water it will be extinguished, is forbidden because it directly prepares the later extinguishing. Where needed, one should place the water there before lighting the candle. It is permitted, however, to insert the candle into sand or a similar substance in such a way that when the flame reaches that place the fuel will no longer burn and the flame will go out by itself. That is considered indirect extinguishing. [Later authorities]

"He gives." See Ateret Zekenim and Taz. Shabbos 153a, and see siman 334, seif 2, and Magen Avraham, letter 3. Nowadays, when according to many authorities we do not have a Torah-level public domain, there is additional room for leniency. The same is written here in letter 3. Regarding carrying less than 4 amot at a time, which is a rabbinic prohibition, one may reason similarly. Telling a non-Jew nowadays is a double rabbinic prohibition, and in a case of substantial monetary loss the Mechaber rules in siman 307, seif 5, according to the first anonymous opinion, that it is permitted.

What the Shulchan Aruch writes, that it is permitted even if he does not pay the non-Jew, appears to refer to a case after nightfall. Before nightfall it is certainly preferable to fix a fee for him. Then the arrangement is permitted in the same way that Beit Hillel permit contracting with a non-Jew before Shabbos. See Rosh at the beginning of Perek Mi SheHechshich. I later saw that Eliyah Rabbah, letters 3 and 4, noticed this point.

See Magen Avraham, siman 261, letter 6, and Responsa Maharshal, siman 46, that during bein hashmashot rabbinic prohibitions are permitted in a case of monetary loss. On Shabbos itself the matter requires study. Magen Avraham, siman 334, letter 3, prohibits in an ordinary case; see there. See also Levush in his gloss, Shaarei Teshuvah, siman 334, Magen Avraham there letters 2 and 17, siman 349, seif 5, siman 362, seif 5 and 17, and the corresponding discussions that will, with God's help, be explained there.
